1	//! The reader's document model — the seam between *what the text is* and *how a
     2	//! surface lays it out*.
     3	//!
     4	//! # Why this module exists
     5	//!
     6	//! The FOCUS reader used to render a **rendering**. The pane chops logical text
     7	//! into fixed-width grid rows, pads every cell, and forgets which breaks were real
     8	//! — then the reader tried to reverse-engineer the original out of that grid. Every
     9	//! recovery step was a guess (was this break width-induced? is this row a code
    10	//! fence? is that indent structure or a margin?), each new guess existed to patch
    11	//! the previous one's misfire, and content that never reached the screen could not
    12	//! be shown at all.
    13	//!
    14	//! The rule this module enforces is: **render from the source, not from another
    15	//! rendering.** The pane and the reader are two *views* of one [`Document`], and
    16	//! neither is derived from the other's layout decisions.
    17	//!
    18	//! # The three pieces
    19	//!
    20	//! - [`Document`] — WHAT the text is. Logical lines, real breaks only. No columns,
    21	//!   no rows, no wrapping. A surface-independent snapshot.
    22	//! - [`DocumentSource`] — WHERE it comes from. Implemented for a terminal pane
    23	//!   today (viewport plus scrollback); an agent's own transcript is the natural
    24	//!   second implementation, and needs none of the recovery below.
    25	//! - [`layout`] — HOW it sits on one surface, at that surface's width. Pure, and
    26	//!   it reports the document position behind every visual row so selection and copy
    27	//!   keep working.
    28	//!
    29	//! # The quarantine
    30	//!
    31	//! [`Document::from_grid_rows`] is the ONLY place that guesses. When text arrives
    32	//! already chopped — because a TUI hard-wrapped its own output before it ever
    33	//! reached the terminal — the original breaks are genuinely gone and no
    34	//! architecture recovers them. Recovery is therefore best-effort *by nature*, and
    35	//! it is confined here rather than spread through the reader. A source that knows
    36	//! its own structure bypasses it entirely.

    38	use gpui::TextRun;

content.text:
## The reader is only as wide as the pane

It draws the pane's own columns and scales them to fill the glass. A 48-column pane opens as 48 columns at 3.65 times the size, about twelve rows at a time, and the slider's smallest setting still draws every letter 1.28 times larger than the pane does. A full-width pane goes the other way: 201 columns at 0.87 times, smaller than the pane itself.

| Pane | Today | Intended |
|---|---|---|
| 201 columns | 0.87x  201 x 53 | 1.0x  175 x 46 |
| 97 columns | 1.81x   97 x 25 | 1.0x  175 x 46 |
| 48 columns | 3.65x   48 x 12 | 1.0x  175 x 46 |

## An agent's reply can't be widened from the screen

Claude Code breaks its own lines and draws every row two columns in, and the reader's healer refuses a row that starts with a space. Measured on the real function: five rows at 48 columns stay five rows, 47 columns wide, in a 150-column reader. Plain shell output, broken by the terminal instead, heals into one line.

```
claude reply: 5 grid rows at 48 cols -> 5 logical lines -> 5 reader rows at 150 cols, widest row 47
```

## Document panes open the shell behind them

Alt+R on a pane showing Markdown, HTML, a PDF, a picture or a video mirrors the terminal that pane was made with, which is hidden behind the document. A floating square already hands its own view to a split without opening the file again, and the reader can borrow the view the same way.
